podcast.title: College and Jobs
podcast.body: Ed O'Brien attended Manchester University. During this period, he held various jobs, including working in a pizza parlor, where physicist Stephen Hawking was a regular customer. He later worked as a bartender and then as someone pouring Earl Grey tea in an old-fashioned tea room. "At O'Brien went to Manchester University."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Origin and Appearance
podcast.body: Ed O'Brien hails from Oxford and is notably "the tall one" among the band members. "Ed O'Brien is also from Oxford. He's the tall one."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Teenage "Porn Provider" Gig (Age 14)
podcast.body: At 14 years old, Ed found a peculiar way to gain popularity among his classmates: he became their provider of porn. This was possible because he was "the only one tall enough to reach the top shelf where they kept the dirty magazines at the local newsstand." His lucrative gig ended abruptly when a copy was discovered on a classmate's bed at boarding school, leading to him being reported. "he was the only one tall enough to reach the top shelf where they kept the dirty magazines at the local newsstand."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Band Formation (1982)
xref.body: The core members, Tom York, Colin Greenwood, and Ed O'Brien, first met and started playing together in their final year at Abingdon, a private school in Oxford, around 1982. At this time, they were approximately 14 or 15 years old. Their initial setup included "three guitarists and a bad drum machine named Dr. Rhythm," and their very first gig was at a friend's birthday party. "Their first gig was at a friends birthday party. This would be sometime in 1982, which means everybody was about 14, 15 years old at the time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Hiatus for College (1991)
xref.body: In 1991, "On a Friday" entered an extended hiatus as all five members pursued higher education at different universities. Ed O'Brien went to Manchester University, Colin Greenwood studied English literature at Cambridge, Phil Selway also studied English literature at Liverpool University, and Johnny Greenwood enrolled in both music and psychology programs at Oxford. Tom York decided to take a year off before attending university. "In 1997, a 1991 on a Friday went on an extended sort of hiatus."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Artist Control vs. Label Business Model
xref.body: Radiohead guitarist Ed O'Brien expressed the band's disillusionment with EMI's new ownership under Guy Hans and Terra Firma, citing Hans's lack of understanding of the music industry and his refusal to meet the band's demands for a new deal. This highlighted the fundamental clash between a creative entity and a strictly profit-driven corporate model. "Here's a quote from guitarist, Ed O'Brien. EMI is in a state of flux. It's been taken over by somebody who's never owned a record company before, Guy Hans and Terra firma. And they don't realize what they're dealing with."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Creative Block and Internal Disagreement (Kid A era)
xref.body: Facing immense pressure for their fourth album, Tom Yorke suffered from burnout and a creative block, unable to write anything. In a January 1999 meeting in Paris, the band had no clear direction. Ed O'Brien advocated for a return to "three minute guitar charge pop songs," a view supported by management. However, the Greenwood brothers and Phil Selway felt "lost," leading to difficult and haphazard recording sessions. "Tom was so freaked out and so burned out that he couldn't seem to write anything."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Intentional Sonic Reinvention (Kid A)
xref.body: For "Kid A," Radiohead intentionally "burned it all down and they started from scratch," fundamentally changing their sound to an electronic record. This involved minimal guitar use by Ed O'Brien and Jonny Greenwood, Phil Selway acting more as a computer programmer, and Tom Yorke creating vocals via self-written computer programs. They successfully "destroyed themselves and rebuilt the band as something brand new." "they burned it all down and they started from scratch, which is not an easy thing to do."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Post-Bends Pressure and Hiatus
xref.body: After the success of "The Bends," Radiohead faced immense pressure to create an even better album, being compared to U2 and R.E.M. To cope, the band members scattered: Ed O'Brien went to India, Tom Yorke traveled solo in Europe, and others stayed home in England. They eventually regrouped in January 1996. "They were being called the next U2 and the next REM."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
